content: The digital system should not merely replace paper registers but should also enhance and streamline processes. It is essential to understand the necessity of each data field and identify opportunities to optimize data flows. Given the extensive data collection required from healthcare providers, it may be more efficient to eliminate data entry fields that do not serve a meaningful purpose for clinicians, public health reporting, or any other identified objectives. Conditional data fields should have clearly defined skip logic. For example, if a data field depends on responses from other fields or can be left blank under certain conditions, the specific skip logic should be documented. This is particularly relevant for follow-up questions. For instance, if the value of one data field falls below a predetermined threshold, certain subsequent data inputs can be skipped. These fields should have skip logic defined by the preset threshold. Aggregate indicators linked to specific data elements should be explicitly identified. If a data element is associated with an aggregate reporting indicator, this linkage should be clearly indicated. Any inconsistencies or issues in the definition of a data field should be noted. These irregularities will need to be resolved later through team discussions and triangulation. This column can also be used for additional notes, annotations, or team communication messages. The copper-bearing intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) is a small, flexible plastic frame with copper sleeves or wire. A trained healthcare provider inserts it into a woman’s uterus through the vagina and cervix. Most IUDs have one or two strings that hang through the cervix into the vagina. The Cu-IUD works by causing a chemical change that damages sperm and eggs before they can meet. The Cu-IUD is one of the most effective and long-lasting contraceptive methods. Fewer than 1 pregnancy per 100 women occurs during the first year of use (6 per 1,000 women with perfect use and 8 per 1,000 women with typical use). This means that 992–994 out of every 1,000 women using Cu-IUDs will not become pregnant. A small risk of pregnancy persists beyond the first year and continues as long as the device is in place. Over 10 years of use, about 2 pregnancies per 100 women occur. Studies have shown that the TCu-380A is effective for up to 12 years, although it is labeled for 10 years of use. Providers should follow national guidelines regarding when the IUD should be removed. Fertility returns immediately after the IUD is removed. However, the Cu-IUD does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The Cu-IUD is safe and suitable for nearly all women, including those who have or have not had children, are married or unmarried, are of any age (including adolescents and women over 40), have recently had an abortion or miscarriage (if no infection is present), are breastfeeding, perform hard physical labor, have a history of ectopic pregnancy, have had pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), have vaginal infections, have anemia, or have mild or asymptomatic HIV (regardless of antiretroviral therapy status). The Cu-IUD must be inserted by a trained healthcare provider. A follow-up visit is recommended after the first monthly bleeding or 3–6 weeks post-insertion. No woman should be denied an IUD solely because follow-up might be difficult or impossible. Some users report changes in bleeding patterns, especially during the first 3–6 months, including prolonged and heavy monthly bleeding, irregular bleeding, and increased cramps and pain during menstruation. Known health benefits include reduced risks of pregnancy, endometrial cancer, and cervical cancer, as well as a decreased risk of ectopic pregnancy. However, uncommon health risks include anemia if the woman already has low iron stores and the IUD causes heavier bleeding. Rare complications include PID if the woman has chlamydia or gonorrhea at the time of insertion, uterine perforation during insertion, and miscarriage, preterm birth, or infection if pregnancy occurs with the IUD in place. The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (LNG-IUD) is a T-shaped plastic device that steadily releases a small amount of levonorgestrel, a progestin hormone. A trained healthcare provider inserts it into the uterus through the vagina and cervix. It is also known as the hormonal IUD and is marketed under brand names such as Mirena, Kyleena, Jaydess, Liletta, and Skyla. The LNG-IUD works by preventing sperm from fertilizing an egg. The LNG-IUD is one of the most effective and long-lasting contraceptive methods. Fewer than 1 pregnancy per 100 women occurs during the first year of use (2 per 1,000 women). This means that 998 out of every 1,000 women using LNG-IUDs will not become pregnant. A small risk of pregnancy persists beyond the first year and continues as long as the device is in place. Mirena and Kyleena are approved for up to 5 years of use, with research suggesting that Mirena may remain effective for up to 7 years. Jaydess, Liletta, and Skyla are approved for up to 3 years of use. Fertility returns immediately after the LNG-IUD is removed. However, the LNG-IUD does not provide protection against STIs. The LNG-IUD is safe and effective for nearly all women, including those who have or have not had children, are married or unmarried, are of any age (including adolescents and women over 40), have recently had an abortion or miscarriage (if no infection is present), are breastfeeding, perform hard physical labor, have a history of ectopic pregnancy, have had PID, have vaginal infections, have anemia, or have mild or asymptomatic HIV (regardless of antiretroviral therapy status). The LNG-IUD must be inserted by a trained healthcare provider. A follow-up visit is recommended after the first monthly bleeding or 3–6 weeks post-insertion. No woman should be denied an IUD solely because follow-up might be difficult or impossible. Some users report changes in bleeding patterns, including lighter bleeding, fewer days of bleeding, infrequent bleeding, irregular bleeding, or no monthly bleeding. Other side effects may include acne, headaches, breast tenderness or pain, nausea, weight gain, dizziness, mood changes, and ovarian cysts. Known health benefits include reduced risks of pregnancy, iron-deficiency anemia, endometrial cancer, and cervical cancer, as well as decreased menstrual cramps, heavy bleeding, and symptoms of endometriosis. Rare health risks include PID if the woman has gonorrhea or chlamydia at the time of insertion and uterine perforation during insertion. Very rare complications include miscarriage, preterm birth, or infection if pregnancy occurs with the LNG-IUD in place. The etonogestrel (ETG) one-rod implant is a small plastic rod, about the size of a matchstick, that releases a progestin hormone similar to natural progesterone. A trained provider performs a minor surgical procedure to place the rod under the skin on the inside of a woman’s upper arm. It does not contain estrogen, making it suitable for use during breastfeeding and for women who cannot use estrogen-containing methods. The implant is labeled for up to 3 years of use.
